Warsh declines forward guidance and says politics played no role. September CPI 3.7% year on year; December hike was about 78% priced before the vote (CME FedWatch via Fortune).
items.fxnote: Provisional: the Warsh-led Board held and Cook voted to hike, which keeps rate control with the Board and weakens the Maximalists' case against Cook; re-score if the Nov 5 hearing or a December cut/hike reverses that.
items.rationale: Net effect (my reading): the Board, not the White House, keeps the rate decision, and its pull is toward tightening, so Trump's push for cuts gets no traction before the election while a December hike stays likely. Cook voting to hike undercuts the picture of her as a Trump-opposed dove, which complicates the Maximalists' Nov 5 case; the hold itself (not a hike) is the Warsh-led majority waiting. Counter-reading: a hold with two hawkish dissents may be Warsh buying time until after Nov 3, so the December hike is not locked. Falsifier: Warsh signals a cut or the Board splits the other way. Tags left empty because no faction clearly gained or lost; the effect falls on the Board and the administration's rate goals. Vote details are consistent across two read sources; Axios and CNBC pages could not be fetched.

items.context: Background: Trump wants to remove Cook, a Biden appointee, for cause over mortgage-fraud allegations she denies; courts have kept her seat, and on Oct 9 the White House set up its own committee hearing as a new route to removal. items.rationale: NET EFFECT (my reading): the US is losing regional influence and the regional support a further strike would need. Three states with US ties (Saudi Arabia, a NATO member, a nuclear power) are treating Iran as a counterpart and building a security arrangement that does not run through Washington. Evidence: they went to Tehran in person under a defence treaty and are mediating; Saudi Arabia told Vance on Jul 29 that Netanyahu pushes escalation; Iran has threatened neighbors' infrastructure, so they bear the cost of a wider war. Not established: any Gulf refusal of basing or overflight, or any private US request they turned down. Counter-reading: the pact lacks enforcement and Turkey says no troops will leave. Mechanics: a strike now has to be justified to a bloc that is mediating and protected by a treaty, which raises the cost and weakens the claim of regional backing. Single analysis, so provisional.

items.context: Trump on Oct 25 framed it as "finish it off or make a deal"; he also accused Iran of inventing ship attacks to lift oil prices before the midterms. The Oct 26 Tehran communiqué only agreed to keep talking: no ceasefire, no deadline, no demands on Washington.
items.rationale: Net effect (my reading): regional mediators now hold a concrete off-ramp that Iran says it welcomes, which raises the political cost of a post-election strike but commits the administration to nothing until it answers. Single anonymous-official source for the draft terms; the US reply is unknown. Counter-reading: Iran may be stalling to outlast the Nov 3 window; falsifier: Iran rejects the draft or Trump publicly accepts the pause. No fx because the direction for any faction is unclear until the US responds.

items.text: Qatari mediators give Iran a draft deal: seven days of daily confidence-building steps by each side, with several guarantor countries. Iran also asks the Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani envoys to press the US for a two-week regional pause in return for gradually reopening Hormuz. Iran is expected to answer by the end of the week; no US response reported.

items.context: Iran told the Tehran visitors it lacks leverage to stop the Houthis. Brent about $113, down from about $116 earlier in the week.
items.rationale: Net effect (my reading): the war is widening into a Saudi-Houthi front that the US is not leading, which ties down Gulf partners and raises oil-price risk for the administration before Nov 3 and for any strike afterward. The Houthi casualty and refinery claims are partisan claims; Egypt's authorization is documented as a parliamentary act. Counter-reading: a Saudi-Egyptian defence line could free US forces; falsifier: US forces are drawn in or Saudi Arabia asks for US basing.
items.text: Houthi offensive on Saudi Arabia escalates: about 97 fighters killed near Bab el-Mandeb, claimed missile strikes on the Ras Tanura refinery, and Egypt's parliament authorizes Sisi to send troops to Saudi Arabia (Houthis call it a declaration of war; Sisi says defensive).

Counter-reading: the carrier signals preparation for post-midterm strikes; falsifier: a second carrier leaves or strike notices appear.

items.text: CENTCOM estimates the Iran war has cost the US military about $47 billion, mostly munitions replacement. On Oct 28 NAVCENT warned ships to stay clear and to expect blockade enforcement, the first such notice since the July blockade began.

items.text: The Pentagon launches FORTRESS: every major continental US base must run essential operations for at least 90 days without civilian power, water, fuel or supply; plans cite microgrids, batteries and portable reactors plus reserves of munitions, fuel and parts. Hegseth unveiled it Sep 30 (SOFX); Parnell defended it publicly (Fox, Oct 25).

Not established: who did it, whether state-backed, any Iran link, whether the incidents are connected to FORTRESS (an aggregator links them by timing only). items.context: Axios reports that Vance previously defended the campaign publicly while privately questioning it and leading negotiations. Donald Trump Jr. publicly backed his postmortem, giving the message a channel into MAGA grassroots audiences. Rubio retains his State Department platform and is a potential rival. Compare https://www.axios.com/2026/11/05/vance-maga-power-play-2028 On Nov 5 Rubio acknowledged the political cost of higher gasoline prices in a New York Times interview, defended Trump’s decision, and denied that he was leaving State to launch a campaign, as reported by AP. https://apnews.com/article/f1e19f47b21ec9dc57d0c4929b29b002 His Oct 31 press availability had defended the administration’s security rationale. https://www.g20.utoronto.ca/2026/261031-rubio-press-conference.html My reading: after Vance’s voter-facing break, Rubio’s national interview reinforces his alignment with Trump and gives Republicans who defend the war a competing postmortem. It also ties Rubio to the war’s costs. Endorsements, polling, personnel and policy remain open. Khanna used the opening to urge attaching an Iran combat funding cutoff to a short-term spending bill. His channel is the incoming House majority and its spending agenda, contingent on leadership and votes. https://english.udayanews.com/congressman-ro-khanna-urges-cutoff-of-iran-war-funding/ Trump publicly welcomed Vance’s post on Nov 4 while defending his own decision to fight.
items.rationale: My reading: Vance’s public break after the election is a credible 2028 positioning move. It lets him appeal to voters alienated by the war and distinguish himself from its architects. The move gives him a clearer electoral argument. Changes in voter support, endorsements and war policy remain unresolved. Trump also acknowledged electoral costs, so the distinction is Vance’s public argument about whether the war was worth the price. Trump Jr.’s backing is for the message. Test durable advantage against candidate endorsements, polling and organizing.

deal-capital.name: Deal-Capital Network
overview: The Deal-Capital Network argues that American power is best used the way a dealmaker uses leverage: wars end when settlement pays better than fighting. Kushner's Abraham Accords are its model, normalization sold through investment and arms. Applied now, Russia is offered asset unfreezing, a Lukoil sale and energy deals for a ceasefire; Iran a negotiated end with no regime change; Venezuela an oil opening run by American firms; the Gulf chips and data centers. In its own best terms this is realism without ideology: no crusades, no forever wars, and American companies first in line for what peace builds.

The interest layer is unusually plain: the negotiators' money is foreign, and mostly Gulf. Affinity Partners reports about 99% foreign capital, led by Saudi Arabia's fund ($2B, about $25M a year in fees) with Qatari and Emirati money (Senate Finance, Jun 2024), and joined the Saudi fund's $55B Electronic Arts buyout. Aryam, Sheikh Tahnoon's vehicle, bought 49% of World Liberty for $500M. Witkoff reported about $107M in 2025 from a World Liberty-linked holding; his son Zach co-founded it, his son Alex runs the Witkoff Group, which sold the Park Lane Hotel to Qatar's fund for $623M (2023). The Trump Organization signed a Qatar golf resort with Saudi Dar Global (Apr 2025). The patrons are sovereigns, so the line tracks what Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Doha want at the time (my reading).

Tested against acts, the 'negotiated deal' line fails on Iran and holds only in form on Russia. On Iran, Witkoff and Kushner held the Geneva talks two days before the Feb 28 strikes; Trump said on Mar 9 his decision rested on 'what Steve and Jared and Pete and others were telling me'; UK officials told the Guardian the envoys acted 'like agents of Israel' when London judged a deal close; Kushner said on Mar 26 Iran had not been serious. Only after the war reached Saudi airports and oil sites did they return as deal brokers (Islamabad Apr 25, Doha Jun 30). On Russia the deal is real but transactional: the Nov 2025 Miami plan with Putin's fund chief Dmitriev put US firms first in line for the frozen $300B, Arctic and Lukoil assets; Aryam sits in the Lukoil bid group; talks move to Abu Dhabi in mid-November; and the pressure falls on Kyiv (the refinery-strike pause Kushner asked for, Oct 29), not Moscow.

Precedent: Taft and Knox's Dollar Diplomacy (1909-13), which used American bank capital to buy influence abroad. It breaks on the direction of the money: then American capital served the state's aims; now foreign sovereign capital funds the American negotiators, so the leverage runs toward the patrons (my reading).

dissenters.name: Article I Dissenters
overview: The Article I Dissenters argue for the constitutional order the founders built: Congress declares war, lays tariffs, writes sanctions and oversees the money, and the president executes the laws Congress passes. Ambition should counter ambition, so a Republican Congress owes a Republican president the same checks it would apply to a Democrat. The program runs across issues: war-powers votes on Iran and Venezuela, ending the Canada tariff emergency, Fed independence, enforcing the Graham sanctions law Trump waived, and forcing out the Epstein files. Its libertarian wing adds restraint abroad and smaller government at home.

What sustains it is insulation and a small libertarian money network, not a donor class. Tillis is retiring, Murkowski and Paul do not face voters until 2028, and Collins's Maine trades heavily with Canada. Jeff Yass has supplied about 95% (~$35M over five years) of Protect Freedom PAC, built by Rand Paul's advisers; it funded Kentucky First ($1.4M for Massie), and Young Americans for Liberty funded another $1.1M. Kentucky 4th PAC's $6.6M came from a new dark-money group (Tamarack Aspen; a straw-donor complaint is pending). The outside wing (Massie, Greene) now lives on audience: Greene left the party (Jun 22) and Massie appears with Carlson ('The movement has begun', Aug 1).

Acts depart from words most where seats are at stake. The Senate core is three votes (Murkowski, Collins, Paul on May 13); Young and Hawley flipped on Venezuela after assurances (Jan 14); the 50-48 Iran win (Jun 23) reversed to 49-50 (Sep 24). Collins votes against tariffs and takes Maine carve-outs, and votes for war-powers limits while taking $100K+ in one quarter from defense-contractor PACs as Appropriations chair. The price of dissent is documented: about $15.5M went against Massie and he lost.

Precedent: Robert Taft's Senate Republicans, who fought Truman's undeclared Korean war on constitutional grounds (1950-51). It breaks because Taft led his party's Senate wing and nearly won the 1952 nomination, while today's dissenters are retiring, losing primaries or leaving the party, and the outside wing's leverage is a third-party threat rather than a nomination path (my reading).

hawks.name: Primacist Hawks
overview: The Primacist Hawks argue that American safety rests on American primacy: hostile regimes that take hostages, sponsor proxies and seek the bomb are removed or broken, not managed (Maduro is gone; Tehran is next); allies that fight their own wars, Israel first, multiply US power; China is denied the chips that would close the gap; Russia stays under sanctions. Credibility is one account, so retreat on one front invites tests on every other. In their own terms this is Reagan's peace through strength, and restraint is what invites war.

The interest layer is a donor network that funds the Republican majorities and disciplines dissent. Miriam Adelson gave at least $67.6M in 2025-26 ($25M MAGA Inc., $30M Senate Leadership Fund, $10M CLF); Paul Singer was the largest donor to the anti-Massie MAGA KY and America 21 ($3M) and gave AIPAC's United Democracy Project its largest individual gift ($2.5M). Pro-Gallrein groups spent about $15.5M and Massie lost (May 19). The Marcus Foundation's $19M to FDD supplies staff and arguments. Defense primes gain from the program (Lockheed's $35B THAAD deal; RTX's $289B backlog), but no contractor payment to the hawk core was found. For Rubio and Cruz the network is the 2028 base; for the Florida delegation it is the exile vote.

Acts depart from words where Trump decides. When Trump signed the June Iran deal, Adelson's Israel Hayom called him a failure (Jun 19) and Levin accused officials of bullying Israel, while the RJC urged trust in Trump (Jun 18) and Rubio sold the deal and told allies there would be no new strikes 'for now' (Aug 25). The access wing follows Trump; the Israel-first wing pushes and loses rounds. maximalists.name: Maximalists
overview: In its own best terms, the Maximalist program is popular sovereignty run through one elected man. The nation is its citizens and its borders; an election hands the president the whole executive; and the permanent government (independent agencies, career prosecutors, a Fed that sets money without answering to anyone, judges who stall removals) is an unelected usurpation to be broken. From that follow the acts: mass deportation (3,000 ICE arrests a day, Oct 6), prosecution of those they see as having weaponized the state against Trump, budget control that starves hostile agencies (Vought's $11B+ in halted projects, Oct 2025), a Fed Board that answers to the president, tariffs as economic sovereignty, and election enforcement as defense of a citizens-only vote. Vought calls it a 'post-constitutional moment' to be corrected; Bannon calls it deconstructing the administrative state; Miller frames it as the nation choosing who belongs. Abroad the doctrine is power, not restraint: Iran must give up its program first, Venezuela is a criminal state.

The interest layer keeps the program running. Most members hold posts that exist at Trump's pleasure (Blanche was his personal lawyer; Patel, Pirro, Pulte), so maximal loyalty is also job security, and each prosecution or referral doubles as an audition for the next post up (Miller and Pulte were floated for Wiles's job, Oct 15). Outside government, a funded pipeline carries the doctrine: Bradley Impact ($27.1M, 2022) and DonorsTrust ($21.3M, 2024) fund Miller's America First Legal; DonorsTrust also funds Howell's Oversight Project. Detention contractors profit from the targets: GEO paid Homan and Venturella before their jobs and gave $4.4M to MAGA Inc. The movement voices now counted here sell the same program to an audience: Bannon's War Room and a possible 2028 run, Loomer's access to Trump, Prince's bid for a privatized removal business.

Acts depart from words in three places. First, 'America First' restraint gives way to loyalty when Trump goes to war: Bannon warned the Iran war could break MAGA and still told CPAC 'people have to have his back' (Mar 27); Loomer branded critics a 'foreign influence operation' (Mar 3); only Prince, whose trade is ground work, dissents. Second, the doctrine of total presidential power bends to the president's own retreats: Trump pulled arrest decisions back to career officials in spring and said Miller 'sometimes goes too far' (Atlantic, May 11), and the faction regained ground only when Trump turned again (Jun 1, Oct 6). Third, the courts: Cook stayed 5-4, the Powell probe closed, both ballot suits lost by Nov 2, and a grand jury refused to indict Cassidy Hutchinson (Oct 27).

Precedent (my reading): A. Mitchell Palmer's 1919-20 raids. An attorney general seeking the presidency used deportation and sedition cases against a 'Red' threat, until Labor's Louis Post cancelled most warrants, a federal court (Colyer v. Skeffington) condemned the methods, and his predicted May Day uprising never came; the drive collapsed with his 1920 bid. It breaks here: Palmer acted alone and against his ailing president's indifference, while the Maximalists hold several agencies at once, have a funded legal arm outside government, and act on the president's own orders, so their limit is Trump's mood and the courts, not a rival cabinet officer.

operation.name: The Operation
overview: In its own best terms the Operation's worldview is that the movement is Trump, and Trump's power is the program. Policies come and go; what lasts is a disciplined political machine that keeps the coalition together (the MAGA base plus the swing voters who returned in 2024), wins elections, and spares the president needless fights. So it runs the campaign through Trump himself, holds the money until it counts (MAGA Inc. held to Labor Day, then about $277M spent by Oct 14), lowers the temperature when the base's demands cost swing seats (quieter raids, no Iran escalation before the vote), and refuses to name an heir. Wiles states it as professionalism: no agenda of her own, only his.

The interest layer: a political machine is also a marketplace for access. Wiles controls Trump's time, so everyone who needs him needs her; an open succession keeps it that way. Blair and LaCivita control the largest pot of money in Republican politics (about $473M raised, 96% from $1M+ donors), and its donors are crypto, energy, AI and casino money with business before the government; several later got posts or pardons for relatives (no causation shown). Their consulting businesses sell Trump-circle proximity abroad: both were paid 'hundreds of thousands' through a law firm retained by Republika Srpska while running Trump's PAC, LaCivita's firm took $1.6M from Albania's opposition, and Wiles's daughter is a partner at a firm that works for Srpska.

Acts depart from words where the business meets the job. Trump called them 'outside consultants' he would 'terminate' if conflicted (Oct 7); the inquiry ended after their fees went to his library (Oct 23), so the remedy was a payment to the principal, not a break with the client. The Operation also loses the fights it says it runs: it wanted quieter raids and the Maximalists got 3,000 arrests a day (Oct 6); Salazar says she warned Blair and Wiles about Latino losses (Oct 31). And its prize asset cannot run again, so the value of controlling access to him starts to decay the day after Nov 3.

Precedent (my reading): Mark Hanna and William McKinley, 1896. A manager raised unprecedented corporate money, set strategy and ran access to the candidate, and his power was the candidate's power. It held while McKinley lived and Hanna kept a Senate seat of his own. It breaks here: Hanna's donors wanted a policy (gold and tariffs) that McKinley also wanted, while the Operation's donors and foreign clients want different things from different parts of government, and its operators hold no office of their own once Trump's term ends.

paras: What happened.

Blair and LaCivita were each paid “hundreds of thousands” through a Washington law firm retained by the Republika Srpska government to advise Milorad Dodik before the Oct 4, 2026 elections (NYT, via Al Jazeera). Srpska has paid more than $4M to Trump-linked lobbyists and operatives since the start of 2025 (DOJ filings).

The US removed sanctions on Dodik and close associates on Oct 29, 2025 (OFAC). Dodik’s travel ban was reportedly lifted in June at the same time as Berisha’s, the Albanian politician LaCivita worked for before Albania’s 2025 elections. Timing is reported; no source proves the lobbying caused it.

Continental Strategy, where Wiles’s daughter Katie is a partner, has been paid $35,000 a month by Srpska since February (DOJ filings). A Continental partner arranged a September White House meeting between Wiles and a Srpska official; Continental says Katie played no role in it.

Katie Wiles went to Srpska in August with John Calce, a Texas energy executive exploring a gas pipeline with the Srpska government. Calce also runs America First Refining, in which Trump Jr. holds a minority stake; Trump endorsed its Brownsville refinery in March, and the company and a predecessor paid Continental $750,000 to lobby the White House and Energy Department (NYT, via DNyuz).

Oct 7: Trump called Blair and LaCivita “outside consultants” and said he would fire them if there was a conflict; he later said there was none. Bannon called them grifters and demanded a review of the money.
Why it is a blunder for the faction. It hands Bannon a weapon and arms the Maximalists. The Operation’s own interest cannot explain it.

Blair Motives: (1) Money: each fee is a payday on top of his MAGA Inc. role. (2) Selling proximity: a Bosnian editor told Al Jazeera the main benefit for Dodik was closeness to Trump, which is a product Blair can only sell while he is in Trump’s inner circle (reported). (3) Exposure: he accepted the risk anyway, which suggests he judged Trump would not punish it.
LaCivita Motives: same as Blair, with a second foreign client, Berisha, who also received travel-ban relief in the same period (reported timing).

Wiles did not take the fees herself. Motives: (1) Family business: her daughter’s firm earns from the same client, so criticizing the operators would expose her family. (2) Access as an asset: the firm’s other client, America First Refining, has Trump Jr. as an investor and a Trump-endorsed project (documented). No source shows Wiles acted on any of it.

Oct 22-23: both gave their Srpska fee (believed over $100,000 each) to Trump's presidential library; LaCivita called it 'an honor and a no brainer', and Trump said his inquiry was over (Daily Beast, citing NY Post). The remedy was a payment to the principal, not an end to the foreign work (my reading).

party.name: Party Machine
overview: In its own best terms the Party Machine's worldview is conventional Republican governance carried inside the Trump era: hold the majorities, because the majority is what turns a movement into law (tax cuts, deregulation, judges, defense budgets); keep the institutions that make the majority durable (the filibuster, the committees, Senate rules); and keep the coalition's two halves, Trump's voters and the party's donors, from splitting. Thune states it as governing; Johnson as protecting the majority and the president together. It sees itself as the adult layer that turns Trump's mandate into votes without losing the seats that make votes possible.

The interest layer: members' seats and leaders' posts, financed by the donor class that predates Trump and outlasts him. SLF and One Nation raised $103M in 2025 and Musk alone gave SLF $158M since July (AP, Oct 12); Adelson, Singer, Mellon and fossil-fuel money fill SLF and CLF. That money lets leaders protect incumbents without Trump, which is why Thune can disappoint him on the SAVE Act and the filibuster and survive Trump's refusal to back him (Jul 30). It also binds leaders to what those donors want: tax and energy policy, a strong defense, and no tariff or war votes that split business from the base.

Acts depart from words on Congress's own powers. The party claims the power of the purse and war but works to avoid using it: leadership tried to bar tariff votes (failed 217-214, Feb 10), Thune could not count 50 for war money (Jul 23), and seven discharge petitions, including the Epstein files, beat Johnson because members would not wait for him. Hawley is the clearest case: a populist against Big Tech in bills that cost him nothing with Trump (AI and chatbots, copyright, layoff disclosure), and a party vote on war powers (Mar 2; Venezuela flip Jan 14).

Precedent (my reading): congressional Republicans and Nixon, 1973-74. Leaders (Hugh Scott, John Rhodes) defended the president while the majority's donors and voters held, then told him he had lost the votes after the 'smoking gun' tape in August 1974. It breaks here: Nixon could not run again and had no primary army, while Trump still decides primaries and his PAC money flows to candidates, so the Party Machine's break point is a midterm loss that shows Trump costs seats, not a scandal.

pentagon.name: Pentagon Network
overview: The Pentagon Network argues that deterrence comes from lethality and industrial mass: a force that can strike Iran within days of an order, a rebuilt munitions and drone base, autonomy and AI fielded at speed, and hard priorities (Colby) that put Iran and China ahead of Europe and make allies pay for Ukraine. Vendors serve the warfighter on its terms ('all lawful uses'), and the state invests directly in the industrial base (a 40% stake in Anduril's shipyard owner, a 35% stake in NABEP). In its own words: peace through strength, rebuilt after decades of drift.

Its interests are budget, posts and vendors. Hegseth's Pentagon sought $200B more for the war ('It takes money to kill bad guys', Mar 19) on top of a $1.5T budget request. Feinberg signed a Mar 9 memo making Palantir's Maven a program of record; Palantir's US government revenue rose 84% in Q1 as Maven use doubled in the war. Anduril holds a $20B Army enterprise ceiling and calls itself a 'heavy participant' against Iran's drones. Lockheed signed a $35B THAAD deal and RTX's backlog hit $289B. Trump's sons' drone makers, SpaceX and xAI sell to it. Feinberg's old firm Cerberus stands to share any Ligado settlement. The FT reported, and the Pentagon denied, that Hegseth's broker sought a defense-stock fund before the war.

Acts depart from 'finish this fight' in one direction: the network keeps the war ready rather than fought. Caine limits the pace on interceptor stocks, Patriots for Ukraine were held and then sold for 2030s delivery, and 'defensive' strikes continue under the pre-election hold (Nov 3). That serves the vendors either way: restocking pays whether or not the big strike comes (my reading). Colby's restraint on Russia and Go Big on Iran are one prioritization, not a contradiction. The Anthropic designation was argued as security; a judge found retaliation (Aug 27) before the appeals court upheld it (Sep 25).

Precedent: the Reagan buildup of 1981-85, a budget surge justified by a rival and spent on new technology. It breaks because the state now takes equity in contractors, the new vendors' founders (Thiel, Musk, Luckey) are political patrons of the people buying from them, and the buyer's own senior officials hold or held stakes (Feinberg, Michael) (my reading).

populist.name: Movement Media and Insurgents
overview: The Movement Media and Insurgents bloc is defined by what its members own, not what they say: audiences outside the government. Carlson owns his network outright after buying out 1789 Capital and the other investors (Axios, Jun 2025). Bannon's War Room airs on Robert Sigg's Real America's Voice; the Mercers cut him off in 2018. Greene and Kent left office and are building a new-party lane with Carlson and Massie (Aug 2026).

Their slogans split by audience. On Iran, Kent resigned citing the war (Mar 17) and Carlson sells restraint, but Bannon told CPAC to "have his back" (Mar 27) and Loomer called war critics a "foreign influence operation" (Mar 3). Loomer, funded by Robert Shillman, depends on access to Trump, so she is re-homed with the Maximalists. Enforcement veterans (Bovino, Morgan, Howell) and the contractor Prince want posts and budget in the deportation machine, which is the Maximalists' interest, so they move there with a secondary row here. Hawley voted against the Iran war powers resolution and flips when the White House presses; he moves to the Party Machine.

Precedent (my reading): Pat Buchanan, a television commentator, ran an "America First" insurgency against a sitting Republican president in 1992, again in 1996, then took the Reform Party line in 2000 and won under one percent. The commentator-to-insurgent-to-third-party path maps onto Carlson, Greene, Kent and Massie: the anti-war line is the product and the leverage, and the exit threat pays only if the party buys it off before it is used.

tech-right.name: Tech-Right
overview: The Tech-Right's program is a nationalist version of the techno-optimism Andreessen set out in 2023: growth and technology make a nation strong, and stagnation is the real danger. Applied to the state, it means winning the AI race against China by letting labs ship without pre-release review and overriding fifty state rulebooks; building the power plants and data centers AI needs; rebuilding the arsenal with software-first firms such as Palantir and Anduril rather than the old primes; putting the dollar on crypto rails; and keeping doors open to engineers. Its best case is that America's edge over China is speed, and every rule is a gift to Beijing.

Each plank is also a portfolio. a16z raised about $15B in January, $1.176B of it for 'American Dynamism' (Anduril, Shield AI, Saronic, Castelion), and Saudi Arabia's Sanabil lists it as a holding (TechCrunch, Jan 9). Founders Fund, Thiel's firm, led Anduril's 2025 round with $1B; Thiel chairs Palantir, whose government revenue rose with the war; Sacks's Craft has 400+ AI-linked investments under ethics waivers; SpaceX takes about a fifth of its revenue from government. The political money is large: Musk gave about $446M and a16z and its founders $116M in the 2026 midterms (NYT via Axios, Nov 2). treasury.name: Treasury and Dollar Statecraft
overview: The Treasury camp holds that America's deepest power is financial: the dollar, the Treasury market every central bank holds, and a Fed whose word markets trust. Spent with care, that power does what armies cannot. Sanctions and licenses squeeze Iran and open or close Venezuela and Russia; tariffs become bargaining chips on legal ground the trade court can uphold; and dollar stablecoins carry the currency into economies whose own money is failing (Bessent, Oct 27). The program is national strength through credibility: no fired Fed chair, no bond rout, managed trade instead of shock, and reindustrialization paced so that markets will fund it. Greer brings the Lighthizer school's case that China trade must be managed, built on Section 301 cases.

Its members' fortunes and careers were made in the markets this program protects. Bessent ran money for Soros and then Key Square; Warsh took $10.2M in fees from Druckenmiller's office and married into the Lauder fortune; Greer was Lighthizer's chief of staff and then a King & Spalding trade partner and lobbyist. Their standing depends on markets believing them, so calm markets are both creed and capital. Turf counts as much: sanctions, licenses and the Treasury-held Venezuelan oil account make Treasury the gate every deal faction must pass. No donor is tied to a position.

Acts depart from words in three places. Sanctions are sold as leverage, yet Treasury's licenses also carry the Deal-Capital track: a diesel license 'at President Trump's direction' (Oct 9) and the Lukoil sale-talks license extended to Nov 21 (Oct 21), so Treasury's own tool serves other people's deals. Fed independence is the creed, yet Warsh and Bessent pursue a new Treasury-Fed accord that pulls the two closer. And Bessent divested his soybean farmland only in the week before he helped announce a $12B farm aid package tied to the China trade fight (Dec 2025): the stake went, but on the eve of a decision it touched.

Precedent: the 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord, when Treasury let the Fed stop pegging bond yields and so created modern Fed independence. It breaks here: Warsh's 'new accord' runs the other way, toward Treasury, while the president attacks a Board whose hike his own chair voted for (my reading).

vance.name: Vance Lane
overview: The Vance Lane argues that the Republican Party should stop serving the bargain of the last forty years: free movement of capital and labor, open-ended wars, and deference to Wall Street and Silicon Valley incumbents. In its own best terms it is a national-conservative, post-liberal program: a state that takes sides for workers, families and places hollowed out by trade ("We won't cater to Wall Street. We'll commit to the working man", Jul 17, 2024); restraint abroad, with Europe paying for its own defense and US power husbanded for China ("No more undefined missions. No more open-ended conflicts", May 23, 2025); immigration cut to raise wages and protect cohesion ("We won't import foreign labor"); and suspicion of concentrated tech and financial power ("It's time to break Google up", 2024). Vance calls himself postliberal (AP, Sep 2024). Carlson is the lane's public voice for the same program; Colby is its doctrine man in the Pentagon.

The interests that sustain it are a challenger-capital network, not old money. Thiel hired Vance, gave $15M to his 2022 race and convened the 2019 Rockbridge summit with him (Carlson and Rebekah Mercer attended); Buskirk runs Rockbridge and co-founded 1789 Capital with Malik, which seeded Carlson's network (Oct 2023) and took Don Jr. as a partner (Nov 2025). The fit is close (my reading): breaking up Google and attacking Microsoft's visa use hurts incumbents that Thiel- and Andreessen-backed firms compete with; restraint in the Middle East plus rearmament for China is demand for Palantir, Anduril and 1789's defense bets; anti-Wall Street talk targets the Griffin and Singer money that leans Rubio. Trump holds the last key: the blessing, which he kept open on Oct 20.

Acts depart from words where Trump or patrons would pay. Vance opposed the Iran strike in private ("no strikes at all", NYT) but defends the war in public (Sep 3), and Colby defended it to the Senate (Mar 3); the restraint shows up as a talks channel (Islamabad, the Oct 28 letter), not a break. His AI line is deregulation (Paris, Feb 2025), which serves the tech patrons more than the anti-Big-Tech words. He raises money at Malik's Hamptons home (Aug 19). The gap costs him his loudest voices: Carlson apologized for backing Trump (Apr 21) and gave a 'shadow run' monologue (Aug 5), and Kent says Vance is 'too compromised' (Aug 5).

Precedent (my reading): Robert Taft's 1952 bid. The nationalist, restraint-minded Midwestern wing, skeptical of permanent alliances, lost the nomination to Eisenhower and the Eastern internationalist money. It breaks in two places: Taft was his own principal, while Vance is an heir who needs a sitting president's blessing; and Taft's base was Main Street business, while Vance's patrons are defense-tech and venture financiers who profit from a larger military, just aimed at China.

Say versus do. A real act, aimed where it costs the lane least; the act is scored to the Maximalists.
IMM.title: Immigration and H-1B

paras: Position.

On July 15, 2024, hours after Trump picked him as his running mate, Vance told Hannity that if the U.S. struck Iran it should strike hard, and cited Trump's strike on Qassem Soleimani approvingly. Later, restraint in private and deference in public. Before the Feb 28 launch Vance 'was for no strikes at all' and warned of regional chaos, a coalition split and the munitions gap (NYT, reported); Trump said he was 'less enthusiastic' (Mar 9). In public: 'punch back' (Jul 8), 'I wouldn't call it a war' (Sep 3). Led the Islamabad talks (Apr) and the Swiss follow-up; letter to an Iranian hardliner (Oct 28, reported); 'progress' (Nov 3).

Later policy goal: avoid opening or widening a Middle East war and preserve capacity for China. Political goal: remain a viable successor to Trump. Leading negotiations advances the restraint agenda and gives Vance a chance to demonstrate leadership while staying in Trump's coalition. That second motive is an inference.
Who and why.

Vance reportedly opposed the initial strikes in private, defended the administration in public, and led talks. Islamabad ended without a deal. The June agreement was a provisional policy gain and collapsed in July. The reported October letter shows renewed outreach. These actions establish a negotiating role. The ledger does not establish a resulting gain in nomination support.

Carlson. Posture: says what Vance argues privately ('disgusting and evil', Feb 28; Vance 'would not be at war with Iran', Jul 17). Interest: owns his network, so the line costs him nothing and grows his audience.
Kent. Posture: no imminent threat, blames Israel's lobby. Interest: resigned at real cost (Mar 17); now his platform is Carlson's lane, which calls Vance compromised.

Thiel backed Vance and called the war a mistake, according to the ledger. Thiel's Palantir stake and defense holdings in the wider 1789 network create financial exposure to military demand. Record that exposure alongside his stated position. The cited material leaves the backers' role in Vance's Iran decisions unresolved. Colby defended the war from inside the Pentagon.
A cut in Israel aid (Trump, Nov 3) is not a lane win: it removes a US brake while the US keeps the exposure (my reading, per the aid-as-leverage lesson).

Evidence: reported pre-strike opposition (NYT, as recorded), Trump's March 9 account, and ledger events irn-2026-04-07-95df20, irn-2026-06-17-205ee7, irn-2026-07-08-51c93a and irn-2026-10-28-vance-letter. Nomination-night interview: https://www.foxnews.com/video/6358113662112.

Stance audit. At his July 2024 rollout Vance backed hard strikes conditionally. He later reportedly opposed the opening strikes privately, defended Trump publicly, and led negotiations. Compare the Hannity interview, the reported private advice and the dated negotiations. The June agreement later collapsed. Succession rewards alignment with Trump. Thiel’s reported war criticism and the defense exposure of some backers point to distinct incentives. Strategic accommodation is a strong reading of the public-private split. Conditional force and opposition to this particular launch can coexist. The evidence leaves the cause of each shift open.
IRN.title: Iran

paras: Position.

Why the faction does it. The program's economics are cost of living for workers; the message softens Trump without contradicting him.
Who and why.
Vance. Posture: the workers' voice on costs. Interest: as RNC finance chair a Nov 3 loss lands on his 2028 record.
Carlson. Proposed restructuring consumer debt (Aug 5): the program's populist edge, stated outside the party.
Say versus do. No act behind the Fed line; the rallies and money are acts.
MID.title: The Fed and the midterm message

paras: Position.
Apr 14: proud of ending aid; with Colby set the burden-shifting line. Oct 21: defended Witkoff. Oct 30: Colby reportedly told a Baltic official Europeans should avoid 'poking' Russia.
Why the faction does it. The program: Europe should pay for its own defense and US power should go to China. It costs no patron, and it keeps Deal-Capital (Witkoff, Kushner) as allies.
Who and why.
Vance. Posture and interest align: restraint is his program and the base's, at no cost to Trump.
Colby. Doctrine, consistently held; his post lets him act on it.
Carlson. Interviewed Putin (Feb 2024) and sells the same line to his audience.
Say versus do. Burden-shifting is an act (Colby); the rest is statement.
RUS.title: Russia and Ukraine

paras: Position.
Undeclared; will talk to Trump after Nov 3. RNC finance chair; raised $5M+ at Malik's home (Aug 19). Leads Rubio 33-23 (NYT/Siena, Oct 24), while Trump holds the question open (Oct 20).

Primary political goal: become president by winning the Republican nomination and inheriting Trump's coalition. Fundraising capacity, endorsements, and a durable turnout network are intermediate gains. Advancing the national-conservative policy program is a separate goal.
Who and why.

Thiel's prior campaign support, the Rockbridge network, and the fundraiser at Malik's home help Vance build a nomination coalition. The RNC finance chair role offers a fundraising platform. For backers around Rockbridge and 1789, access and influence in a future administration are plausible political returns. Their portfolio interests are separate financial stakes. Trump's eventual endorsement remains unresolved in the export.

Don Jr. Pushed the 2024 pick (CNN, Jul 2024); hub of the restraint bloc (Semafor). Interest: 1789 partner (Nov 2025) and adviser to firms that later got government benefits; a Vance presidency keeps the family's access (my reading). CREW found no clear quid pro quo.
Buskirk. Runs Rockbridge and co-founded 1789, whose portfolio firms reportedly won $70M+ in Pentagon contracts (Warren's office).
Carlson. Pushed the 2024 pick; 'I'll support the best person' (Jun 25). Interest: he owns his audience and keeps a 2028 exit open, so he is both kingmaker and possible spoiler.
Kent. Urged Carlson to run because Vance is 'too compromised' (Aug 5): on succession his acts serve the outside wing.
Surabian, Chabria: careers rise with Vance. Erika Kirk: Turning Point's influence.

Observed gains: the RNC finance role and the reported August fundraiser. Thiel's September statement indicates continued support. These establish organization and backing. The nomination and presidency remain open. Evidence: suc-2025-03-58b7aa, suc-2026-08-19-b59801 and suc-2026-09-24-11ac54.

Nov 7 nominee/faction consistency review: the public Nov 4 Iran postmortem supplies an immediate succession argument, while earlier war defenses leave credibility exposure. Don Jr.’s backing concerns that message. Do not wait for a policy change to recognize positioning, and do not claim measured support gains. Evidence: irn-2026-11-04-vance-postelection-war-critique. This updates the pre-election succession paragraph above.
SUC.title: Succession

paras: Position.
Doubted the raid beforehand ('all of us were kind of skeptical', said afterward); cast the 51-50 tie-break that blocked the war powers resolution (January); 'stolen oil must be returned'.
Why the faction does it. The program dislikes regime change, but the vote was Trump's to win.
Who and why.
Vance. Posture: defends the raid. Interest: the blessing; the tie-break is the clearest act of public deference on record.
Say versus do. Doubt in words; the act backed the operation.

Stance audit. Vance expressed skepticism about the raid and then cast the tie-break against the war-powers resolution. The vote is a consequential act. The retrospective remark describes skepticism but does not date or define a prior commitment to the resolution. Loyalty to Trump can protect succession standing. The ledger supplies no evidence of donor direction on this vote. Behavior favored Trump when institutional restraint was at stake. Political accommodation is plausible. The remarks and vote address different decisions.
VEN.title: Venezuela

vance.wants: Win the presidency by becoming Trump's successor and building a nomination coalition. Separately pursue tighter immigration, policies favoring workers and families, competition with incumbent technology firms, and restraint abroad with a focus on China.
vance.weak: The program and the patrons pull apart on visas and defense spending; the restraint voices (Carlson, Kent) are drifting to a third party; and Trump, not the lane, holds the blessing (Oct 20)
vance.why: Political power is the central prize. Thiel's backing and the Rockbridge and 1789 Capital networks supply money, turnout capacity, and access. Their technology and defense investments create policy stakes that can pull against restraint or other program goals. Track Trump's endorsement, donor support, and policy concessions separately. Malik's role as fundraiser host and his ties to Vance's donor network give him and his circle a channel into the succession coalition. That is political representation through access and coalition building. The relationship matters independently of any contribution by Malik or 1789 Capital. Influence over individual policy decisions needs decision-specific evidence.
vance.win: Led the Islamabad talks (Apr) and the Swiss follow-up after the June memorandum (Jun 17); RNC finance chair and the Aug 19 fundraiser

rules: Roster: Add a standalone person only when a tracked decision establishes material authority, implementation, backing, or influence. Keep incidental mentions in event text and case participants in the legal record. Check structured links before pruning.

Representation: Record whose interests have a channel through access, fundraising, organizing, personnel, or financial ties. Identify the backer and recipient. Verify the kind of tie and distinguish announced, awarded, paid, and realized amounts.

Stance changes: Compare dated positions, audiences, decisions, and consequential acts. Record what the actor or backer stood to gain, what else changed, and any counterexample where the actor held a position at a cost.

Motives: Assess power, money, access, ideology, loyalty, status, audience, and survival on their own evidence. Record competing explanations and distinguish a documented benefit, an inferred motive, and evidence of influence.

Authority and scoring: Identify who decides, blocks, implements, and influences. Link each episode across relevant issues and count it once overall. Separate stages and score policy, access, formal authority, succession, and financial gain independently. Preserve legacy scores for comparison. Withhold credit when the relevant outcome or prior goal lacks support.

vance.basis: Compare the Hannity interview, the reported private advice and the dated negotiations. The June agreement later collapsed. Strategic accommodation is a strong reading of the public-private split. Conditional force and opposition to this particular launch can coexist. The evidence leaves the cause of each shift open.
vance.gain: Negotiating access and a provisional June agreement. The agreement later collapsed. A succession gain from diplomacy remains unestablished.
vance.motive: Succession rewards alignment with Trump. Thiel’s reported war criticism and the defense exposure of some backers point to distinct incentives.

MID.alternative: Fire the operators and reset the message
MID.decision: Spend the MAGA Inc. war chest on a Trump-centered message and keep the operators (Blair, LaCivita) after the Srpska inquiry was closed Oct 23

dissenters.basis: House GOP candidates ran no tariff ads; Collins thanked the White House for the Canada rollback (Reason, Oct 26).
dissenters.gain: Little: Trump's low approval pulls them down.
dissenters.motive: Swing-seat Republicans like Collins and Rogers distance themselves from tariffs and the war to survive.

maximalists.basis: DOJ v. California ballots (Oct 15) and Alaska suit (Oct 22-23): the Ninth Circuit (Oct 30) and the Supreme Court (Nov 2) rejected ballot segregation, an Oct 30 TRO (to Nov 16) bars DOJ threats, and Judge Gleason dismissed the Alaska suit (Nov 1).
maximalists.gain: Criminal probes continue (LA County grand jury Nov 4, Alaska inquiry) and the Omar search stands, but both ballot suits have lost in court and a judge threw out the Floris-Benavides case as 'weaponization' (Nov 2).
maximalists.motive: Use DOJ and DHS actions as election tools and as auditions for senior jobs; enforcement keeps their base energized.

operation.basis: Daily Beast citing NY Post (Oct 23); Trump said the inquiry was over; Democrats lead 47-36 (Reuters/Ipsos, Oct 22-26).
operation.gain: Operators stay after the Srpska fee went to Trump's library (Oct 23); about $277M spent by Oct 14.
operation.motive: Keep control of the campaign money and message so blame for Nov 3 lands elsewhere; the operators' jobs, access and outside consulting value depend on it.

party.basis: Close Senate races in Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Kansas (Al Jazeera, Oct 28); Cook moves 12 more House races toward Democrats (Oct 30).
party.gain: Committee money flows to close Senate races.
party.motive: Hold House and Senate seats; committees need the war chest and a message that does not tie members to Trump's 32% approval.

TAR.alternative: Broad cuts or quick deals with Canada and Mexico on steel and autos before the vote
TAR.decision: Keep the wall high (Section 301 wall, 50% metals, 25% autos, Section 338 on Canada) while reshaping the Canada list before Nov 3 (22 lines off, 100 on, in force Oct 30); China truce to Jan 10, 2027

deal-capital.basis: Mexico deal stalled (Oct 15); Trump's $54B Korea LNG claim disputed by Seoul (Oct 2).
deal-capital.gain: 50% on metals held; Mexico deal stalled on Lutnick's terms; Korea LNG pledge touted.
deal-capital.motive: Protect metals for industrial allies and keep investment-for-tariff deals flowing that dealmakers can announce and broker.

dissenters.basis: Section 338 edits effective Oct 30 (CNBC, Flexport); Canada emergency ended in the House 219-211 (Feb 11).
dissenters.gain: Maine carve-outs (plywood, cardboard) in force Oct 30, but 100 lines were added and the wall stays.
dissenters.motive: Trade-exposed Republicans like Collins want relief for home-state industries to keep their seats.

maximalists.basis: Opposed Mexico cuts (Oct 15); 232 proclamations Oct 22 and 28.
maximalists.gain: High tariffs stand, the Canada list grew by 100 lines (Oct 30) and new Section 232 sectors open (robotics Oct 28, wind Oct 22), though without rates.
maximalists.motive: Navarro and allies keep their standing with Trump by holding the protectionist line.

operation.basis: Trump approval 32% (Reuters/Ipsos Oct 22-26); August deficit widest since early 2025 (Oct 6).
operation.gain: Little: tariffs keep prices up; only targeted Canada relief.
operation.motive: Wiles's team wants lower prices to carry the midterm message and avoid blame for losses.

party.basis: Vote bar failed 217-214 (Feb 10); GOP candidates ran no tariff ads (Reason, Oct 26).
party.gain: Some Canada relief before the vote, but the Oct 30 edit added 100 lines (air conditioners, power tools), so prices and the 32% approval still weigh on them.
party.motive: Leaders want no tariff votes and some visible relief before Nov 3 to protect swing seats.

treasury.basis: Section 301 wall (Jul 24); truce to Jan 10 (Sep 23); case argued Sep 30, ruling pending.
treasury.gain: The Section 301 wall stands pending a ruling and the China truce holds.
treasury.motive: Keep tariffs that survive the trade court and do not shock markets; Bessent keeps market credibility and Greer keeps trade authority in USTR.

VEN.alternative: An early dated election (Machado's Jul 24, 2027 proposal or sooner) with a faster handover of power
VEN.decision: Keep Rodríguez in office and Machado out; elections only after court and electoral-council overhauls (best case June 2027); oil sales continue through a Treasury-controlled account

deal-capital.gain: Oil sales proceed with no election date set.
deal-capital.motive: Oil access and deal flow for Wright's and the envoys' circle: barrels and contracts move now, before any election can reopen them.

dissenters.motive: Swing-seat and retiring members want oversight of military action without a fight with Trump before Nov 3.

hawks.gain: State sets the timetable and the terms Rodríguez must meet.
hawks.motive: Rubio keeps State in charge of the transition and a foreign-policy win for 2028, while holding the Florida Venezuelan-American vote that wants Machado in.

pentagon.gain: The 35% NABEP stake stays in place.
pentagon.motive: Hegseth and Feinberg keep the Pentagon's own oil-deal stake and revenue stream, which a new government could renegotiate.

treasury.gain: Control of the Treasury-held oil account and the delisting tool.
treasury.motive: Bessent keeps the licenses and the oil-revenue account in Treasury's hands, which makes Treasury the gate for every deal.

motives.note: Evaluate power, money, ideology, loyalty, audience, status, survival and institutional duty as separate possible motives. Record donor support and donor stakes by recipient and issue. Evidence of a benefit establishes an incentive. Evidence of a motive or decision influence requires its own basis. Existing diff scores compare the current decision with the main alternative and await a separate scoring audit.

patterns.note: Cross-event patterns the daily task found by comparing events across issues. Each is a hypothesis labeled my reading; none claims money or motive caused a decision. Needs at least three dated, independent items; each states a test and what would retire it.

patterns.disproof: Retire if the Graham sanctions are enforced or Hawks win a Russia decision.
patterns.label: my reading
patterns.summary: Three shifts in six weeks each helped Deal-Capital and hurt the Hawks: the Graham sanctions law signed then waived (Sep 18), the diesel deal (Oct 9), the Witkoff-Putin meeting with a Kremlin offer to rejoin talks (Oct 21). Week of Oct 26 adds: Kremlin confirms talks on sanctions relief for its investment fund (Oct 29), Kyiv pauses refinery strikes under US pressure (Oct 29), envoys pitch Russian gas transit through Ukraine (Nov 2). Counter: State approves a $2.1B Patriot sale to Ukraine (Oct 31).
patterns.test: Supported if the Lukoil licence is extended past Nov 21 or three-way talks resume in mid-November.
patterns.title: Russia file moving from sanctions camp to the envoys

patterns.disproof: Retire if the cap is shown to be a purely commercial or technical decision.
patterns.label: my reading
patterns.summary: Cap hits Ukrainian drones (Oct 13); the WSJ says Musk ordered it (Oct 20); Trump calls Musk and Kyiv later says speeds are restored (Oct 21-24). Hegseth and Rubio call it a commercial matter. Tech-Right gains on Russia in the same window.
patterns.test: Supported if SpaceX or the White House confirms a link between the cap and negotiations.
patterns.title: Starshield speed cap used as a lever in the Russia track

patterns.disproof: Retire if Trump endorses Vance or tech donors publicly recommit.
patterns.label: my reading
patterns.summary: Three weak succession signals in seven weeks (Sep 1 donors prefer Rubio, Sep 24 Thiel hedges, Oct 20 Trump leaves Vance-or-Rubio open), while Vance backs eliminating H-1B (Oct 2) against his tech donors' interest and Microsoft rebuts him (Oct 14).
patterns.test: Supported if tech donors publicly shift away from Vance or he softens on H-1B.
patterns.title: Vance squeezed between his restrictionist base and tech donors

patterns.disproof: Retire if the delay is explained by another cause or deliveries resume during Iran escalation.
patterns.label: my reading, weakest
patterns.summary: Hegseth appears in eight Iran events (secret Israel trip, threats if talks fail) and five Russia events (Patriot transfer held Oct 19 then denied). Possible resource trade-off with Gulf needs. Oct 29: allies fear Patriots for Ukraine are held until after Nov 3; Oct 31: State approves a $2.1B Patriot sale paid by Ukraine and partners (a sale, not deliveries, so the disproof is not met).
patterns.test: Supported if Ukraine deliveries resume only after Iran de-escalates.
patterns.title: Hegseth hard on Iran, slow on Ukraine arms

patterns.disproof: Retire if the Supreme Court grants DOJ relief on the California ballots or a grand jury indicts in one of this fall's voting probes.
patterns.label: my reading
patterns.summary: In one week, seven separate rulings or refusals went against DOJ actions on voting and on Trump critics: Hutchinson no-bill (Oct 27), Essayli ruled unlawfully serving (Oct 27), Ninth Circuit ballot rulings (Oct 26, 30), Thompson order on threats to election officials (Oct 30), Rochon ads order (Oct 30), Alaska suit dismissed (Nov 1). DOJ keeps opening new probes (Arizona Oct 30, North Carolina charges Oct 29), so volume rises as wins fall.
patterns.test: Supported if the Supreme Court denies the California ballot application and the Alaska appeal fails before certification.
patterns.title: Courts and grand juries check the enforcers' pre-election legal push

patterns.disproof: Retire if none of them happens by Nov 30, which would mean the deferrals were about the talks, not the vote.
patterns.label: my reading
patterns.summary: Several moves were put off to the same date: Gulf states told to prepare for a short US campaign after Nov 3 (Oct 28); Ukraine pauses refinery strikes until after the vote to keep fuel prices down (Oct 29); allies fear Patriots are held until after Nov 3 (Oct 29); US and Israel weigh large strikes after Nov 3 (Oct 30); Trump says no new Iran attacks before the vote (Nov 1); Netanyahu presses for strikes right after the midterms (Nov 2). The common thread is fuel prices and the vote, not the merits of each file.
patterns.test: Supported if by Nov 17 at least two of the deferred moves happen (a US strike on Iran, resumed Ukrainian refinery strikes, Patriot deliveries released).
patterns.title: Decisions across Iran and Russia deferred to 'after Nov 3'

pipes.note: Documented money, stake or pay is a filled dot. Reported, indirect or conduit-only is a ring. Dissenters: Massie got $2.5M against $15M+ on the other side; no pipe. Money shows role-payer fit; no source shows a payment caused a decision.

policy.AI: AI rules stay light: the administration wants federal law to override state AI laws, backs chip exports, and asks only for a voluntary 30-day safety review.
policy.EPS: The Justice Department has released about 3.5 million of roughly 6 million Epstein file pages and says that meets its legal duty. Others want the rest.
policy.FED: Trump is trying to take control of the Federal Reserve by removing officials like Governor Lisa Cook; courts have so far kept her seat.
policy.IMM: Deportation pushes continue at about 3,000 arrests a day, and processing of employment-based green-card applications (PERM) is suspended.
policy.IRN: The U.S. holds off on a renewed campaign against Iran through Nov 3 but carried out unannounced 'defensive' strikes on Iranian missile sites; plans for a larger attack are ready.
policy.MID: AP projects Democrats will take control of both chambers in the next Congress. Track outstanding race calls, certification, and congressional leadership elections.
policy.RUS: The administration is easing some sanctions on Russia (a law waived Oct 16, a diesel license Oct 9) while pursuing a peace deal.
policy.SUC: Trump hasn't picked a 2028 successor. Vice President Vance leads, but his lead has narrowed.
policy.TAR: Tariffs stay high on most imports; the Canada tariff list was reshaped before the election (some goods off, more on), and Mexico relief is still being negotiated.
policy.VEN: The U.S. keeps Rodríguez in place and excludes Machado; elections only after court and electoral-council overhauls, best case June 2027; oil money goes to a Treasury-controlled account.

stances.note: One-line what/why per faction per issue, written from the Oct 24 reports. First line = what they push for and how; second = why and who backs it. Stance audit entries assess selected episodes by actor and issue. Coverage records where the three views overlap.

deal-capital.what: Sells chips to Gulf partners: H200 sales; Mythos controls imposed then lifted (Jun 12-30); license-free chips to the UAE (Jul 10). Interest: Gulf funds that back the envoys' firms and Lutnick's family data-center deals.
deal-capital.why: Documented fit: Aryam and MGX ties to World Liberty, Cantor's $310M Nvidia stake; the White House denies a chip link.

hawks.what: Chip curbs written into law, 42-2 (Jan 22); OVERWATCH in the NDAA (Jul 14).
hawks.why: China hawkishness. No donor tied to this position.

maximalists.what: Hassett floated FDA-style review in May and accepted the narrower June approach. Bannon continued to criticize the labs.
maximalists.why: Alignment with Trump can protect appointment prospects. The ledger ties no specific backer to Hassett’s shift. A retreat in policy posture is visible. Preserve the internal split and distinguish accepting the final policy from securing it.

operation.what: Pressed the Jun 2 voluntary review order; Wiles rebuked FDA-style licensing and met Amodei Apr 17.
operation.why: AI splits Trump's coalition; a voluntary order lets him act without choosing a side (my reading).

party.what: Hawley pursued restrictions while other Republicans, including Cruz on state preemption, took different approaches.
party.why: Electoral positioning and industry backing are plausible incentives. Map each contribution or policy stake to its recipient. Treat this as a faction split. The evidence for a common leadership position or individual reversal is thin.

pentagon.what: All lawful uses from AI vendors: Anthropic designated (Feb 27; upheld Sep 25); Maven made a program of record (Mar 9); Grok on its networks.
pentagon.why: Documented acts; Feinberg's memo reported (Reuters). Palantir's US government revenue +84% (Q1). Power over vendors and vendor gains coincide.

tech-right.what: The ledger groups preemption, less review, and chip sales under one agenda.
tech-right.why: a16z, Brockman, Founders Fund and Nvidia have different political or portfolio stakes. Export revenue and strategic limits on China can diverge. Split the planks before judging consistency. Campaign support and financial exposure alone leave policy influence unresolved.

treasury.what: Convened bank CEOs on Mythos (Apr 7) and pressed the Jun 2 order.
treasury.why: A model-driven bank breach is a direct market risk (my reading).

vance.what: Program: distrust Big Tech power ('break Google up'). Posture on AI: no rules, labs' requests a 'Trojan horse'. Interest: no-rules AI and antitrust on incumbents both serve Thiel, Andreessen and 1789 bets.
vance.why: Documented: 2024 Google post; Feb 2025 Paris speech; Sep 14 remark. No act found. Fit with patrons (my reading).

dissenters.what: Forced the Epstein Act (427-1). Massie lost his seat after $15.5M against him; Greene left the party and makes the files her outside content.
dissenters.why: Documented (WKMS FEC data; Washington Examiner). A cross-party grievance that now sustains an outside platform (my reading).

maximalists.what: Declared DOJ's duty met (Jan 30) and said the files 'should not be a part of anything going forward'; lost a D.C. Circuit stay bid on the foreign-language file review (Oct 28).
maximalists.why: Close the case to protect Trump.

operation.what: No act; Wiles says Trump is 'in the file but nothing awful'.
operation.why: The story threatens Trump's standing, and the Operation's authority rests on it.

party.what: Contain it: Johnson called the petition moot; Comer said DOJ 'botched' the release.
party.why: Comer's criticism of DOJ is his only public distance.

vance.what: Program: elites should not escape accountability. Posture: Vance says nothing was hidden; Carlson says cover-up. Interest: any Vance act would cross Trump.
vance.why: Documented: Jul 15 Rogan remarks; no act found. Carlson's line is content for an audience he owns (my reading).

dissenters.what: Block Fed nominees until the Powell probe closed (Tillis, Apr 24); protect the Board's independence.
dissenters.why: Protect Congress's and the Fed's independence. No donor stream behind it.

maximalists.what: Put the Board under the president: Pulte's referral and firing letter for Cook, Powell subpoenas. Cook stays 5-4 and voted for a hike Oct 28.
maximalists.why: So the Board cuts rates and the president's picks govern. Courts have held so far: Cook stays 5-4.

treasury.what: Treasury favored market credibility and sought a closer accord. The FOMC voted on rates.
treasury.why: Borrowing costs and institutional influence are Treasury stakes. The ledger records professional financial ties and identifies no issue-specific donor. Preserve both the credibility and influence objectives. A rate result alone gives no evidence of a Treasury stance reversal.

vance.what: Program: cost of living for workers. Posture: the Fed should cut (Sep 3), 'we hear you' on costs. Interest: repeats Trump at no cost and keeps RNC donors calm.
vance.why: Documented: Sep 3 remark; no act. Costless alignment with Trump (my reading).

dissenters.what: Paul withheld the Schroyer hearing; Salazar ran an ad; Tillis blames Miller.

maximalists.what: Posture: the nation decides who belongs. Interest: control of ICE (Venturella, Jun 1), a legal arm funded by Bradley and DonorsTrust, and contractors' beds. 3,000 a day ordered Oct 6 after a spring pullback.
maximalists.why: Documented grants: Bradley $27.1M (2022), DonorsTrust $21.3M (2024). Reported: Atlantic (May 11) on the spring pullback. Contractor tie is a documented fit, no causation.

operation.what: The political team reportedly wanted a lower profile for raids before the election. The October 6 arrest directive moved the other way.
operation.why: Electoral risk and control of the agenda are separate stakes. MAGA Inc. backers fund electoral capacity. A reported timing preference and a setback. Evidence of a public reversal or donor direction is missing.

tech-right.what: Musk vowed 'war' for H-1B (Dec 2024), later softened; silent on the fee and PERM suspensions since.
tech-right.why: A skilled-visa pipeline serves tech employers, but a public fight is costly for those who depend on the government.

vance.what: Program: restrict immigration to raise wages. Act: PERM suspensions (Oct 8) hit Microsoft, Adobe and outsourcers, incumbents his venture patrons compete with; patrons still want skilled visas open.
vance.why: Documented: Oct 2 remark, Oct 8 suspensions, Oct 17 recast. Aimed where it costs the lane least (my reading); the act is scored to the Maximalists.

deal-capital.what: Negotiators moved from prewar talks and reported input to Trump before strikes to brokering a settlement.
deal-capital.why: Brokerage preserves access. Gulf investment and business ties create exposure to regional escalation. A change in role is established. A donor-directed reversal remains unsubstantiated. War and its regional effects changed the bargaining problem.

dissenters.what: Members repeatedly sought war-powers votes while the coalition and vote counts shifted.
